sentences.text: The genus name Iguanacolossus combines the word for the modern reptile Iguana with the Latin word for giant, referencing its large body size and iguana-like teeth. The specific name fortis means mighty.
Iguanacolossus was a large, robust dinosaur estimated to reach 9 meters in length and weigh 5 tonnes.
The preserved maxilla of Iguanacolossus has 14 alveoli, suggesting an elliptical and elongate antorbital fossa.
The two right metatarsals of Iguanacolossus are identified as metatarsals III and IV based on comparisons with Camptosaurus and Iguanodon.
The holotype specimen UMNH VP 20205 was discovered by Donald D. DeBlieux in 2005 in the Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation in Utah.
Iguanacolossus was formally named and described in 2010 by a team including Andrew T. McDonald, James I. Kirkland, and Donald D. DeBlieux.
Additional juvenile remains, including lower jaws and humeri, found at the Doelling's Bowl site are currently under revision.
Iguanacolossus lived alongside theropods like Falcarius and Geminiraptor, the sauropod Mierasaurus, and the turtle Naomichelys in the Lower Yellow Cat bed.
Indeterminate goniopholidids are known from the same Lower Yellow Cat environment as Iguanacolossus.
Iguanacolossus is classified within the Iguanodontia, specifically as a styracosternan, a basal subgroup that includes Hadrosauridae and dinosaurs closer to hadrosaurs than to camptosaurs.
The right pubis of Iguanacolossus displays both derived and primitive features found in related iguanodontians.
Iguanacolossus lived approximately 130 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous (Barremian stage) in what is now North America.
The time range for Iguanacolossus is estimated from 139.1 to 132.6 million years ago, spanning the Berriasian to Valanginian stages.
